issue_context.title: Add the new meta-data from system-info.sh to the web API and ACLK.
issue_context.body:
# Feature idea summary

The `system-info.sh` script will be updated in #7731 to add the following new information

*    Number of cores
*    Nominal frequency (not the current frequency)
*    Amount of RAM
*    Sum of available capacity on disks

The format of these new environment variables will be defined. The data needs to be read into `main.c` where the script is called, stored in an appropriate place and then included in the `/api/v1/info` response as new fields, and in the `info` metadata message on the ACLK. For this task only the web API handler needs to be updated - the ACLK functionality calls that handler.

##### Expected behavior

We should be able to see the new information in `/api/v1/info` queries on a range of systems that includes different processor architectures (ARM, AMD, Intel) and different types of netdata installation (bare-metal, VM, container).

review_comments: I don't like how rrdhost_set_system_info_variable() always frees whatever is in every system_info field, relying on the undocumented fact that if something hasn't been set yet it should be NULL. Moreover, it relies on `freez()` being a no-op on NULL values. We will get bitten by this.
Why is this a problem? What do you think will go wrong?

Somebody could call `rrdhost_set_system_info_variable()` without having zeroed the structure.

Also, `freez()` is not documented to handle NULL arguments.

One solution is to document both functions. E.g.

```
// system_info fields must be heap allocated or NULL
rrdhost_set_system_info_variable(struct rrdhost_system_info *system_info...)

// If ptr is NULL, no operation is performed.
freez()

```

I understood your point of view @mfundul , and I will add an `if` before to free the information.
We did not change this before, because this was the original code and we only brought the necessary variables.
Something analogous what I am bringing is also done inside health
Wait, you don't need an `if`, what do you mean exactly?

I commit now the changes, please, take a look.
This pattern that I brought here is used inside `health/health_config.c`, but it was not present in this file.

I saw the change, this doesn't solve anything:
1. If the `system_info` structure is NOT zeroed out you will corrupt the memory anyway
2. If the `system_info` structure IS zeroed out then you gain nothing because `freez()` was already safe because it calls `free()` inside that is safe according to documentation.

1 . System_info is zeroed inside `stream/rrdpush.c` and `daemon/main.c`, there is not way Netdata will arrive in this point with any value.
2 . Sure, but we have two different "patterns" on our code, one used in health, that is possible to be reloaded during runtime, and another here. I added the `if` for we have only one pattern in our code. I agree that it was not necessary to add `ifs` now, but it can be in the future.

1. That's the point, we may add calls in the future.
2. The `if`s don't add anything, cause if it's NULL `freez()` works anyway. If it's random garbage, then the `freez()` will corrupt the memory equally with or without an `if`.
I agreed with `1.` and `2.`, so I am keeping the `if` for case we start calling this function during runtime, and I also added the suggested documentation.

Please remove the ifs again - they are redundant as there is a check inside `freez()`. @mfundul While your point is technically true it is not helpful in this case. The whole of the Netdata codebase operates on the assumption that `callocz` is used to allocate data-structures specifically so that they are zero'd out as their initial state. There is no code-path in which the contents of that structure are uninitialized. Whilst you may disagree with this policy as it exists globally within the entire code-base - this PR is not the place to address it.

Edit: the check is not directly in freez() but it is documented as part of the interface to free().

Are you sure ?

https://github.com/netdata/netdata/blob/4dc217a48a0b337e1f0baa13faa93a12c575a500/libnetdata/libnetdata.c#L171

:D
Ah, geez... yes I had checked that and saw there is a check -- BUT failed to see that works only if NETDATA_LOG_ALLOCATIONS is set -- thanks @thiagoftsm :smile:

Is there a specific reason that we expose (and store cores, ram and cpu freq) as strings? 
In general everything is exposed as strings (except the alarms object)
Since I began to work with Netdata, this was the pattern, I believe this happens, because the protocol used to send the response is a text protocol by definition.
Pretty certain we're using JSON, which absolutely supports integer and floating-point values.

You are correct @Ferroin , we are using JSON that has these supports, an important question for both, before I bring possible changes. Case we decide to do this on Netdata side, this will bring more processing to the web server every time that it generates the response, should we do this?

I just remembered why we would want these to be strings. If the script that gives this data to the core can't figure out values for these, it returns 'unknown' as a string, so we need to support passing that on.
All right, I will keep it as text for while.
